topics.title: Coasts: erosion and landforms
topics.intro: The sea is a sculptor. Waves attack cliffs in four ways, carve caves into arches and stacks, and carry sand along the beach grain by grain.
topics.teach: Explain how a cave becomes a stack.
topics.talk: Next time you are at a beach, ask her which way the groynes show the sand is moving.

topics.title: Development: measuring how countries differ
topics.intro: How do we compare rich and poor countries fairly? Geographers use indicators: income, life expectancy, literacy, infant mortality. Each tells part of the story.
topics.teach: Explain why income alone is not a good measure of development.
topics.talk: Ask her which single number she would use to decide how well a country looks after its people.

topics.title: Weather systems: pressure, fronts and forecasts
topics.intro: Why does the UK get so much changeable weather? Low pressure brings cloud and rain; high pressure brings clear skies. Fronts are the battle lines between warm and cold air.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between high and low pressure weather.
topics.talk: Look at tonight’s weather map together and find the fronts.

topics.title: World: harder countries and capitals
topics.intro: Beyond the famous names: eighteen more countries that a well-travelled mind should be able to place on a map.
topics.teach: Point to three countries on a world map that most people could not find.
topics.talk: Ask her the capital of Mongolia (it is a tongue-twister).

items.prompt: Which statement about waves is true?

options.text: Waves are made by wind blowing across the sea
Waves are caused by the pull of the Moon
options.feedback: The Moon causes tides, not waves.

options.text: Waves carry water right across the ocean
options.feedback: Energy moves across; the water mostly goes round in circles.

items.explain: The distance wind blows over open water is called the fetch. A long fetch (the Atlantic hitting Cornwall) means big waves.

items.prompt: Which type of erosion is the sheer force of waves smashing into cracks and compressing the air inside?
items.explain: Hydraulic action: water and trapped air are forced into cracks, which widen until the rock breaks.

items.prompt: Waves hurling sand and pebbles against a cliff, wearing it away like sandpaper, is called…
items.explain: Abrasion (also called corrasion) is the sandpaper effect.

items.prompt: Pebbles knocking against each other and becoming smaller and rounder is called…
items.explain: Attrition is why beach pebbles are smooth: they wear each other down.

items.prompt: Put the stages of headland erosion in order.
items.explain: Waves widen a crack into a cave; the cave breaks through the headland into an arch; the arch roof collapses, leaving a stack; the stack is worn down to a stump.

items.prompt: Why do headlands and bays form along some coasts?

options.text: Soft rock erodes faster than the hard rock beside it
Rivers cut the bays as they reach the sea
options.feedback: It is the sea eroding softer rock faster.

options.text: People dig out the bays to make harbours
options.feedback: Harbours use natural bays; they do not create them.

items.explain: Where rock types alternate along the coast, the sea picks out the soft rock. Swanage Bay and Durlston Head in Dorset are a classic example.

items.prompt: What is the zigzag movement of sand along a beach, driven by waves hitting at an angle, called?
items.explain: Waves swash up the beach at an angle and drain straight back; each wave moves sand a little further along.

items.prompt: A long, narrow ridge of sand built out from the coast by longshore drift is called a…
items.explain: Spurn Head in Yorkshire is a spit 5 km long.

items.prompt: What are the wooden or stone walls built across a beach to trap sand called?
items.explain: Groynes stop longshore drift carrying the beach away. The sand piles up on one side, showing the direction of drift.

items.prompt: A village on a crumbling clay cliff asks for a sea wall. Which is a GOOD reason to say no?

options.text: It would starve beaches further along of sand
Sea walls never work against strong waves
options.feedback: They work, at a cost. The issue is knock-on effects.

options.text: Small villages are not worth protecting
options.feedback: That is a value judgement, not a geographical reason. Decisions weigh costs against the value of what is protected.

items.explain: Protecting one stretch of coast often starves another of sediment. Some places now choose “managed retreat”.

items.prompt: Which country is most developed, and which indicator tells you LEAST on its own?

options.text: A; income alone can hide inequality
C, because low income means simpler lives
options.feedback: Development measures how long and healthy lives are. Country C has the shortest lives and highest infant deaths.

options.text: It is impossible to tell from these figures
options.feedback: Every indicator points the same way here: A, then B, then C.

items.explain: Geographers combine indicators (the Human Development Index uses income, life expectancy and education) because any one number can mislead.
items.passage:
Development data for three countries (rounded)

Country A: income per person $65,000 · life expectancy 81 · 99% of adults can read · 6 babies in 1,000 die before age 1
Country B: income per person $9,000 · life expectancy 73 · 92% of adults can read · 22 babies in 1,000 die before age 1
Country C: income per person $800 · life expectancy 59 · 44% of adults can read · 70 babies in 1,000 die before age 1

items.prompt: In Country C, 70 babies in every 1,000 die before their first birthday. What percentage is that?
items.explain: 70 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 7%. Infant mortality is one of the most sensitive measures of development.

items.prompt: Why is life expectancy such a useful development indicator?

options.text: It sums up health, food and safety in one number
Because it is easy to guess for any country
options.feedback: It is calculated from careful records of births and deaths.

options.text: Because it only measures how rich people are
options.feedback: Nobody does, but people in richer countries live about twenty years longer on average.

items.explain: A long average life needs clean water, enough food, vaccinations, doctors and peace. It captures a lot at once.

items.prompt: Which UN measure combines income, life expectancy and years of schooling into one number between 0 and 1?
items.explain: HDI: Norway and Switzerland are near 0.96; the lowest countries are below 0.4.

items.prompt: What does GDP per capita measure?
items.answer: the value a country produces per person
distractors: the number of cars per family
the average wage of factory workers
the amount of gold a country owns
items.explain: Per capita means per head. It is the most common measure of wealth, but it says nothing about how equally the wealth is shared.

items.prompt: What do the letters LIC stand for in geography?
items.explain: LICs, NEEs (newly emerging economies such as Brazil and India) and HICs (high-income countries) replaced the old “third world” labels.

items.prompt: As countries develop, birth rates usually fall. Why?

options.text: More children survive and more girls are educated
Governments everywhere ban large families
options.feedback: A few have tried, but the fall happens everywhere development happens.

options.text: People stop wanting children at all
options.feedback: Families get smaller, not childless. Education of girls is the strongest single factor.

items.explain: The demographic transition: high birth and death rates, then death rates fall, then birth rates follow.

items.prompt: A country sells raw cocoa beans for $2 a kilo. The chocolate made from them sells for $20 a kilo abroad. What does this show about development?

options.text: Processing goods earns far more than raw materials
Cocoa beans are almost worthless to anyone
options.feedback: It is valuable, but most of the value is added later by processing and branding.

options.text: Chocolate makers charge far too much abroad
options.feedback: The point is where the value and jobs end up.

items.explain: Many LICs export raw materials cheaply and import manufactured goods dearly, which makes it hard to grow richer. Fair trade schemes try to shift the balance.

items.prompt: Which kind of pressure system brings cloud, wind and rain to the UK?
items.explain: Air rises in a low, cools, and its water vapour condenses into cloud and rain.

items.prompt: Which kind of pressure system brings clear skies, light winds, hot summer days and frosty winter nights?
items.explain: In a high, air sinks and warms, so clouds cannot form. Clear nights lose heat quickly: frost in winter.

items.prompt: What is the boundary between a mass of warm air and a mass of cold air called?
items.explain: Warm fronts bring steady rain as warm air slides up over cold; cold fronts bring short heavy showers as cold air undercuts warm.

items.prompt: On a weather map, what are the lines joining places with the same air pressure called?
items.explain: Close isobars mean a big pressure difference over a short distance, which means strong winds.

items.prompt: Where are winds strongest on a weather map?

options.text: Where the isobars are closest together
Where the isobars are far apart
options.feedback: Widely spaced isobars mean a gentle pressure gradient and light winds.

options.text: At the centre of a high
options.feedback: The centre of a high is usually calm.

items.explain: Wind is air moving from high to low pressure. The steeper the pressure change, the faster the wind.

items.prompt: Why is UK weather so changeable?

options.text: It sits where warm and cold air masses meet
Because it is a small island in the sea
options.feedback: Being an island matters (mild, wet), but the changeability comes from the fronts and depressions passing over.

options.text: Because of the Gulf Stream and nothing else
options.feedback: The Gulf Stream keeps the UK mild, not changeable.

items.explain: The polar front runs near the UK. Depressions form along it and are steered east by the jet stream.

items.prompt: From which direction does the UK’s prevailing wind blow?
items.explain: South-westerlies off the Atlantic: mild and moist, which is why the west is wetter than the east.

items.prompt: A forecaster sees a deep low approaching from the Atlantic with tightly packed isobars. What should she expect?

options.text: Strong winds and heavy rain
A long, dry heatwave
options.feedback: Heatwaves come with high pressure.

options.text: Calm weather with fog and frost
options.feedback: Those need calm, clear conditions: a high.

items.explain: The Met Office names storms when a deep depression is likely to cause damage. The deeper the low, the tighter the isobars, the stronger the wind.
